questions.bookRef: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.explanation: Atomicity means all-or-nothing: a transaction that cannot commit is aborted and its writes discarded, so retrying is safe. Keeping the debit would leave a partial write, and auto-completing the credit risks applying it twice — neither is atomicity's guarantee.
options: Keep the debit and let the application credit B later when it retries
Undo the debit so the transaction has no effect, allowing the application to safely retry
Automatically complete the credit to B during crash recovery
Ask the operator whether the partial debit should be kept
questions.question: A funds-transfer transaction debits account A, then crashes before crediting account B. Under atomicity, what must the database do?

questions.bookRef: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.explanation: Consistency here means the application's invariants (e.g. debits equal credits) — only the app knows them. The database provides atomicity, isolation, and durability, which the application uses to preserve its own consistency.
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
questions.question: In the ACID sense, which property is the application's responsibility rather than the database's?

questions.bookRef: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.explanation: Single-object writes are typically atomic already, so grouping queries is not automatically a transaction. Real transactions are needed when several objects must change together or not at all — the classic multi-account transfer.
options: When updating a single document with one write operation
When incrementing a single counter through the database's atomic increment
When one business operation must update several records atomically, such as moving money between two accounts
Whenever a session runs more than one query in a row
questions.question: When do you actually need a multi-object transaction?

questions.bookRef: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
questions.explanation: Durability is the promise that committed data survives crashes, realized as non-volatile storage on one node or replication to enough nodes in a cluster. It is not an absolute guarantee against every catastrophe (e.g. correlated failures destroying all replicas).
options: Once a transaction commits, its writes must survive a subsequent crash
In a single-node database, durability typically means the data reached non-volatile storage such as a disk or SSD
In a replicated database, durability may mean the data was copied to some number of nodes
Durability guarantees committed data can never be lost under any circumstances
questions.question: Which statements about durability are true? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Read committed prevents exactly two anomalies: dirty reads and dirty writes. The snapshot description belongs to snapshot isolation, the serial-order description to serializability, and read committed still permits lost updates.
options: Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot for its entire duration
Lost updates are impossible
You only read committed data, and you only overwrite committed data
Concurrent transactions appear to execute in some serial order
questions.question: What does the read committed isolation level guarantee?

questions.explanation: Atomic operations, explicit locks, and conflict detection (including compare-and-set) all serialize the competing updates. Read committed is the classic trap: it prevents dirty writes but still allows two transactions to read the same value and clobber each other's update.
options: Using the database's atomic increment operation instead of read-modify-write
Explicitly locking the row before the read-modify-write cycle
Relying on read committed isolation alone
Compare-and-set, or automatic detection that aborts on concurrent modification
questions.question: Two transactions both read a counter (value 10), increment it, and write back 11 — a lost update. Which techniques can prevent this? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: This is write skew: the reads overlap but the writes touch disjoint objects, so no write-write conflict is detected. Snapshot isolation does not prevent it — that is precisely why write skew is dangerous. The fix is serializable isolation or materializing the conflict.
options: A lost update, which read committed would have prevented
Write skew, which is still possible under snapshot isolation
A dirty read, which snapshot isolation would have prevented
A phantom read, which only two-phase locking can prevent
questions.question: Two doctors are on call. Each checks the rota, sees the other is on call, and signs themselves off — leaving nobody on call. What is this anomaly, and which isolation level still allows it?

questions.explanation: Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot via MVCC. But 'repeatable read' is a naming trap — its meaning varies by database — and snapshot isolation famously does not prevent write skew.
options: Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken when the transaction began
It is typically implemented with multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)
'Repeatable read' means the same isolation semantics in every database
It prevents write skew
questions.question: Which statements about snapshot isolation are true? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Serializability is about the observable effect matching some serial execution — not about literally running one at a time (that is just one implementation strategy, serial execution). Lock-free, non-blocking behavior is not part of the guarantee.
options: Transactions literally execute one at a time on a single thread
The effect of concurrent transactions is the same as if they had run in some serial order
No transaction ever has to wait for a lock
Reads never block writes and writes never block reads
questions.question: What does serializable isolation guarantee?

questions.explanation: 2PL allows shared read locks but exclusive write locks, with writers blocking readers — the source of its performance cost. Locks are held until the transaction ends (that is the 'two phases'), and 2PL is famously deadlock-prone; phantoms additionally need predicate or index-range locks.
options: Readers never block writers, so reads are always fast
Many transactions may hold read locks on the same object, but only one may hold the write lock, and a writer blocks readers
Locks are released as soon as each individual statement finishes
Deadlocks are impossible because locks are always acquired in a fixed order
questions.question: In two-phase locking (2PL), which statement is correct?

questions.explanation: SSI's optimism is its performance advantage over 2PL, but aborts are its mechanism — it kills transactions exhibiting dangerous patterns (stale reads, writes affecting prior reads). The application must therefore handle retries; 'never aborts' describes nothing real here.
options: It is optimistic: transactions proceed without blocking, and one is aborted if a dangerous pattern is detected
It detects decisions based on an outdated premise — stale MVCC reads, and writes that affect a prior read
It never aborts transactions, unlike two-phase locking
Applications using SSI must be prepared to retry aborted transactions
questions.question: Which statements about serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) are true? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: The chapter frames the whole topic as a deliberate trade-off: serializability costs performance, so weaker levels exist — but you must know what each permits. Serial execution is the simplest correct approach, limited by scalability (see Serializability). Read committed is the dangerous default: it still allows lost updates and write skew.
options: Weaker isolation levels exist mainly because serializability carries a performance cost
You should know which anomalies each isolation level permits before choosing one
Running transactions literally one at a time (serial execution) avoids concurrency control but is difficult to scale
Read committed is always a safe default because it prevents every race condition
questions.question: Which statements reflect this chapter's guidance on transactions and isolation levels? (select all that apply)

summary.overview: This chapter treats transactions as the database's core correctness abstraction: a way to group reads and writes so the application can ignore most concurrency bugs and partial failures. It unpacks the vague ACID slogan, climbs the ladder of isolation levels from read committed through snapshot isolation to full serializability, and shows exactly which race conditions each level still permits. It matters because the wrong isolation level silently corrupts data while full serializability costs performance — so you must know which anomalies your workload can tolerate.

sections.heading: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction
takeaways: A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit: either all of them succeed (commit) or all are undone (abort/rollback), so the application can safely retry without fearing partial writes.

Atomicity means an aborted transaction's writes are discarded; durability means a committed transaction's writes survive crashes — on a single node that means non-volatile storage, on replicated systems it means the data reached enough nodes.

In the ACID sense, consistency is the application's property (its invariants, e.g. debits equal credits), not the database's — the database supplies atomicity, isolation, and durability for the app to build on.
Single-object writes are usually atomic already; you need real multi-object transactions when one business operation must update several records atomically, like moving money between two accounts.

sections.heading: Weak Isolation Levels
takeaways: Read committed guarantees no dirty reads (you only see committed data) and no dirty writes (you only overwrite committed data) — typically via row locks for writes and keeping old and new versions for reads.

Snapshot isolation gives every transaction a consistent snapshot to read from, usually implemented with multi-version concurrency control (MVCC); beware that 'repeatable read' means different things in different databases.

Lost updates — two transactions reading the same value and both writing back — are prevented by atomic write operations, explicit locking, automatic conflict detection, compare-and-set, or conflict resolution in replicated systems; read committed alone does not stop them.

Write skew is subtler: two transactions read overlapping data, decide, then write disjoint objects (e.g. two on-call doctors each seeing the other on call and both signing off). Snapshot isolation does not prevent it; use serializable isolation or materialize the conflict into a single row both must update.

sections.heading: Serializability
takeaways: Serializability is the strongest isolation level: concurrent transactions behave as if they had executed in some serial order, which rules out every race condition including write skew.
Actual serial execution — running transactions strictly one at a time, often via stored procedures — needs no concurrency control at all, but it is hard to scale; partitioning can help.

Two-phase locking (2PL) lets many transactions read simultaneously but gives only one the write lock, with writers blocking readers; it is deadlock-prone and slow, and stopping phantoms needs predicate or index-range locks.

Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) is optimistic: transactions run without blocking, and one is aborted when a dangerous pattern is detected — a decision based on a stale read, or a write affecting a prior read — so applications must retry aborted transactions.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Transactions are an abstraction layer that frees the application from most concurrency and partial-failure worries; weaker isolation levels exist because serializability costs performance.
Choose your isolation level deliberately: know which anomalies each level permits, and when in doubt prefer serializable (or SSI) and design the application to retry aborted transactions.
